title: Robots at Home and in the City
tagline: The robots you can already meet — in your home, your street, and your city.
description: Ten lessons on the robots already around us: vacuum and lawn-mowing robots, window and pool cleaners, cooking and delivery robots, warehouse robots, surgical robots, toy kits, AI-driven robots, and service robots in shops, hotels and hospitals.
outcome: After this course you can explain how the everyday robots around you actually sense, move and work, and tell a real smart robot from a scripted toy.
whoFor: Anyone who has used or seen a robot vacuum, delivery robot or hospital robot and wants to know how it really works.
prerequisites: None. No maths or coding needed.
outcomes: Explain how a robot vacuum and a robot mower each find their way around
Describe what cooking, delivery and warehouse robots actually automate
Explain clearly that a surgical robot is controlled by a surgeon, not autonomous
Tell a genuinely programmable robot kit from a scripted toy
Describe where AI language models fit into a robot's control system

finalActivity.title: Spot a robot's real job
finalActivity.prompt: Think of a robot you've seen in a shop, hotel, hospital or on the street. Write one sentence on the specific task it does, and one sentence on what it is NOT able to do on its own.

lessons.title: How a Robot Vacuum Finds Its Way Around Your Home
lessons.summary: See how bump sensors, lasers (LIDAR) and mapping let a robot vacuum cover a room without a human steering it.

quiz.q: How do many modern robot vacuums build a map of your home?
options: Using LIDAR or cameras to scan the room and build a floor plan
By asking the homeowner to draw a map
They never build any map
quiz.why: Many current models use laser (LIDAR) or visual mapping to understand room layout rather than moving at random.

quiz.q: What does a bump sensor help a robot vacuum do?
options: Detect a collision and change direction
Measure the floor's temperature
Charge the battery
quiz.why: A bump sensor tells the robot it has hit something, so it can turn and continue cleaning.

quiz.q: Why do robot vacuums often get stuck on cables or loose socks?
options: Their sensors can struggle to detect thin, low-lying or soft obstacles
They are programmed to stop on purpose
They cannot move at all on carpets
quiz.why: Thin cables and soft fabric are harder for typical sensors to reliably detect compared to furniture or walls.

quiz.q: Why is building a map useful, beyond just avoiding walls?
options: It lets the robot clean efficiently and remember which areas are already done
A map has no real benefit
Maps are only used for marketing photos
quiz.why: A stored map lets the robot plan efficient paths and avoid repeating the same spot unnecessarily.

lessons.title: Lawn-Mowing Robots: How They Stay in the Garden
lessons.summary: Learn how a boundary wire — or newer GPS-based systems — keeps a robot mower inside your garden.

quiz.q: What has traditionally kept a robot mower from wandering out of the garden?
options: A buried boundary wire that the mower detects and turns back from
A person walking behind it the whole time
Nothing; it just guesses
quiz.why: A perimeter wire emits a signal the mower senses, so it knows where the lawn ends.

quiz.q: What is a newer alternative to boundary wires in some robot mowers?
options: GPS or satellite-based positioning for wire-free boundaries
A long rope tied to a tree
Nothing; wires are the only method that has ever existed
quiz.why: Some newer models use satellite positioning to define boundaries without burying any wire.

quiz.q: Why do robot mowers usually mow in short, frequent sessions rather than one long cut?
options: Frequent light trims keep the grass healthier and need less power per session
It is required by law
Longer sessions are impossible for any mower
quiz.why: Frequent light mowing is gentler on the grass and spreads out battery use.

quiz.q: What sensor commonly helps a mower avoid cutting itself on an obstacle like a rock?
options: Collision or lift sensors
A smell sensor
A sound-only microphone
quiz.why: Collision detection (and lift sensors that stop the blade if tilted) protect both the mower and the obstacle.

lessons.title: Window and Pool Cleaning Robots
lessons.summary: Understand suction and tracked wheels for window robots, and navigation underwater for pool-cleaning robots.

quiz.q: How does a window-cleaning robot usually stay attached to a vertical glass surface?
options: Suction or vacuum pressure holding it to the glass
Strong magnets that work on any surface
It does not stay attached; a person holds it
quiz.why: Most window robots use a vacuum/suction mechanism to grip smooth glass as they move.

quiz.q: What happens to many window-cleaning robots if the power cuts out?
options: A backup system (like a battery-powered suction or safety tether) usually keeps them from falling
They always fall immediately with no backup
Nothing changes about their operation
quiz.why: Reputable window robots include battery backup for suction or a safety tether, precisely because losing grip would be dangerous.

quiz.q: How does a pool-cleaning robot typically move and navigate underwater?
options: Tracked wheels or propulsion driven by a program or sensors mapping the pool shape
It floats randomly with no control at all
A diver manually pushes it around
quiz.why: Pool robots use powered tracks or thrusters along with internal logic to cover the pool systematically.

quiz.q: What's a key design difference between a window robot and a pool robot?
options: A window robot must grip a vertical surface; a pool robot must work fully submerged
They are identical machines used interchangeably
Neither robot uses any sensors
quiz.why: Each is engineered for a very different physical environment — vertical dry glass versus fully submerged water.

lessons.title: Robot Chefs and Cooking Robots: What They Can Really Do
lessons.summary: See what cooking robots actually automate today — and why judging doneness is still a hard sensing problem.

quiz.q: What do most current cooking robots automate well?
options: Repetitive steps like stirring, flipping or precise ingredient dispensing
Inventing brand new recipes from imagination
Tasting food and deciding if it needs more salt
quiz.why: Robots excel at repeatable, precisely timed actions; judgment calls like taste are still hard.

quiz.q: How can a cooking robot judge when food like onions are done?
options: Sensors like cameras, colour detection or temperature probes, combined with timing
It always guesses randomly
It cannot judge this at all, ever
quiz.why: Visual and temperature sensing paired with programmed timing helps approximate what a human chef judges by eye and smell.

quiz.q: Why is taste and texture judgment still a hard problem for robots?
options: These are subtle, subjective senses that are difficult to replicate with current sensors
Robots are not allowed to cook food
All foods taste identical to sensors
quiz.why: Taste and texture involve nuanced human perception that current sensor technology only approximates.

quiz.q: Where are cooking robots currently most useful commercially?
options: High-volume, repeatable food prep like fast food or central kitchens
Fine dining where every dish must be totally unique each time
Nowhere; no cooking robots are deployed commercially
quiz.why: Repeatable, high-volume preparation suits current robot capabilities better than highly varied creative cooking.

lessons.title: Delivery Robots on Pavements and in Restaurants
lessons.summary: See how sidewalk delivery robots sense pedestrians and crossings, and how restaurant robots navigate tables.

quiz.q: What sensors help a sidewalk delivery robot avoid pedestrians?
options: Cameras and distance sensors (like LIDAR) detecting people and obstacles
No sensors; people must move for it
A loudspeaker that scares everyone away
quiz.why: Delivery robots use cameras and ranging sensors to detect and avoid people and objects in real time.

quiz.q: How does a sidewalk robot typically handle crossing a street?
options: It slows or stops, checks for traffic using sensors, and crosses when clear (often cautiously)
It always runs through traffic at full speed
Crossing streets is never attempted by any delivery robot
quiz.why: Road crossings are high-risk, so these robots are typically conservative, checking carefully before crossing.

quiz.q: How does a restaurant delivery robot usually find its way between tables?
options: Pre-mapped floor layout combined with sensors to avoid chairs, people and other obstacles
Random movement with no planning
A staff member drives it manually every trip
quiz.why: Restaurant robots typically use a stored map of the floor plus live obstacle sensing to navigate between tables.

quiz.q: What is a current limitation of pavement delivery robots?
options: They can struggle in bad weather, crowded areas, or unusual obstacles like construction
They can deliver to literally any location on Earth instantly
They need no navigation system at all
quiz.why: Unusual, messy or crowded environments remain harder for current delivery robots than clear, familiar routes.

lessons.title: Warehouse Robots: How Online Orders Get Packed
lessons.summary: Follow an online order through a modern warehouse, where robots bring shelves to people (and increasingly, to other robots).

quiz.q: In many modern warehouses, what do mobile robots do instead of a worker walking to a shelf?
options: Bring the whole shelf or pod to the worker's station
Nothing; all shelves are still fetched manually everywhere
Only deliver snacks to workers
quiz.why: 'Goods-to-person' systems use robots to bring shelving units directly to a picking station, saving walking time.

quiz.q: What helps warehouse robots avoid colliding with each other in a busy aisle?
options: Centralized traffic coordination plus onboard obstacle sensors
Nothing; collisions are common and expected constantly
They never operate near each other
quiz.why: A coordinating system plans robot paths to avoid conflicts, backed up by each robot's own collision sensors.

quiz.q: Why do robotic arms often handle the final pick-and-pack step for certain items?
options: For items with predictable shapes, a robot arm can grasp and pack repeatably and fast
Arms are only used for cleaning floors
Packing is always done entirely by hand everywhere
quiz.why: Repeatable item shapes are well suited to robotic grasping, which speeds up the packing stage.

quiz.q: What part of warehouse fulfilment is typically hardest to automate fully?
options: Handling a huge variety of irregular, fragile or unusually shaped items
Moving a shelf in a straight line
Reading a barcode
quiz.why: Great variety in item shape, size and fragility is still a major challenge for fully automated picking.

lessons.title: Surgical Robots: What the Robot Really Does in an Operation
lessons.summary: Clarify that a surgeon controls the robot's arms directly — the robot does not operate on its own.

quiz.q: Does a surgical robot like the da Vinci system operate on its own?
options: No — a surgeon controls its arms directly from a console throughout the operation
Yes, it fully decides and performs surgery with no human involved
It only works if no surgeon is present
quiz.why: Surgical robots are teleoperated tools: the surgeon's hand movements directly drive the instrument tips.

quiz.q: What advantage does a surgical robot's arm often give over a human hand alone?
options: Finer, steadier movement and a wider range of motion through small incisions
It replaces the need for any surgeon training
It makes incisions larger
quiz.why: Robotic arms can filter hand tremor and rotate instruments in ways a human wrist alone cannot, enabling precise minimally invasive surgery.

quiz.q: Why are surgical robots usually used for minimally invasive procedures?
options: Smaller incisions with precise robotic tools can mean less trauma and faster recovery
They only work through very large open incisions
Incision size has no bearing on their use
quiz.why: A major benefit of these systems is enabling precise work through small incisions, aiding faster patient recovery.

quiz.q: What is the surgeon's role during a robot-assisted operation?
options: Actively controlling every movement of the instruments from a console
Simply watching while the machine decides everything
Only present in case the robot asks a question
quiz.why: The surgeon is in active, continuous control the entire time — the system is a sophisticated steering tool, not an autonomous decision-maker.

lessons.title: Robot Toys and Kits: What Is Smart and What Is Not
lessons.summary: Tell the difference between simple pre-programmed toy robots and real programmable educational kits.

quiz.q: What usually makes a toy robot only 'seem' smart?
options: It follows a small set of fixed pre-programmed reactions, not real decision-making
It contains a full research-grade AI model
It was built by a university lab
quiz.why: Many toy robots have a limited library of canned responses rather than any flexible reasoning.

quiz.q: What makes an educational robotics kit genuinely different from a basic toy?
options: It's programmable, letting the user write and change its actual behaviour
It is always more expensive, which is the only difference
It has more stickers on the box
quiz.why: A real kit exposes programmability, so behaviour comes from code the learner writes, not a fixed factory script.

quiz.q: Why might a parent check whether a 'smart' toy robot is actually programmable?
options: To judge whether it will teach real skills or just repeat fixed canned actions
Programmability makes no difference to the toy's educational value
All robot toys are identical in capability
quiz.why: If the goal is learning, true programmability (versus fixed scripted behaviour) is the key differentiator.

quiz.q: What's an example of a genuinely programmable beginner kit mentioned in this course?
options: Kits like LEGO Mindstorms, which let users write real programs
A plush toy with a recorded voice line
A plastic figure with no electronics
quiz.why: LEGO Mindstorms and similar kits let beginners actually write and test programs, unlike simple scripted toys.

lessons.title: AI Robots: How a Chatbot Gets a Body
lessons.summary: See how a large language model is connected to a robot's sensors and motors to turn chat into physical action.

quiz.q: What role does an AI language model typically play when connected to a robot?
options: Interpreting instructions and planning, which is then translated into motor commands
Directly controlling every motor's exact voltage with no other software
Replacing all of the robot's physical hardware
quiz.why: A language model usually handles high-level understanding and planning, while separate control software executes precise motor commands.

quiz.q: Why can't a chat-focused AI model alone safely control a robot's motors?
options: It isn't designed for the precise, fast, safety-critical control loops motors need
Chat models already perfectly control motors with no other software
Robots have no motors to control
quiz.why: Safe, precise real-time motor control needs dedicated control systems; a language model provides reasoning, not millisecond-level motor signals.

quiz.q: What's a realistic task for an 'AI robot' combining a chatbot and a robot body today?
options: Understanding a spoken instruction and planning a simple multi-step action
Performing any task perfectly on the first try with zero errors
Replacing a surgeon with no other systems involved
quiz.why: Current systems can reasonably interpret instructions and plan simple actions, though reliability and complexity are still limited.

quiz.q: Why is grounding an AI model's understanding in real sensor data important for a robot?
options: Without real sensor feedback, the model's plans may not match the robot's actual surroundings
Sensors are unnecessary if the AI model is large enough
Grounding only matters for text chatbots, not robots
quiz.why: A plan based on outdated or missing sensor data can lead the robot to act incorrectly in the real world.

lessons.title: Robots in Shops, Hotels and Hospitals
lessons.summary: Tour service robots already working in the real world: greeting, delivering, cleaning and assisting.

quiz.q: What's a common role for a robot in a retail shop today?
options: Monitoring inventory shelves or assisting with simple customer questions
Fully replacing every human employee instantly
Cooking meals in the stockroom
quiz.why: Shop robots today are commonly used for things like shelf-scanning and basic customer assistance, alongside human staff.

quiz.q: How does a hotel delivery robot typically move between floors?
options: It can be integrated with elevator systems to call and ride lifts on its own
It is carried by hand up every flight of stairs
It cannot move between floors at all
quiz.why: Many hotel robots are integrated with building elevator systems so they can autonomously travel between floors.

quiz.q: What's a typical role for a robot in a hospital, besides surgery?
options: Transporting supplies, medicines or samples between departments
Making medical diagnoses with full legal authority, unsupervised
Replacing nurses entirely
quiz.why: Hospital logistics robots commonly handle transport tasks, which frees up staff time rather than making medical decisions.

quiz.q: What do shop, hotel and hospital service robots mostly have in common?
options: They work in structured indoor spaces doing specific, repeatable support tasks
They all fly using propellers
They require no sensors whatsoever
quiz.why: These service robots typically operate in controlled indoor environments doing narrow, well-defined support jobs.
